title: Latency-Budgeted Surge Curator PRD (draft)
content:
Context and problem statement:

We offer Dedicated pools that provide predictable throughput and data isolation. Customers increasingly want controlled burst capacity but are also sensitive to tail latency spikes when noisy tenants oversubscribe GPU headroom. Existing burst mechanisms are binary (allow/deny) or credit-based without explicit latency awareness. That lets some tenants hit their burst allowance but causes 95th/99th latency regressions for other customers.

Proposal (one-liner):
Introduce a Latency-Budgeted Surge Curator (LBSC): a controller that mediates burst allocations per-tenant by consuming precomputed latency budgets rather than raw compute tokens. The curator accepts short spikes while ensuring per-pool latency SLAs by adaptively throttling or rerouting requests before tail-sla breaches.

Goals:
- Primary: Keep 95th/99th token generation latency within configured SLOs for each Dedicated pool during short-term demand spikes.
- Secondary: Provide tenants predictable, discoverable burst behavior and clear accounting (latency budget units consumed).
- Tertiary: Minimize failed requests and reduce noisy-neighbor fallout without heavy-handed eviction.

Non-goals:
- This is not an immediate replacement for long-running scale-outs; steady-state capacity scaling remains the autoscaler’s responsibility.
- Not intended to change per-token pricing; pricing model changes are out-of-scope for initial rollout.

Key concepts and terminology:
- Latency Budget Unit (LBU): an abstract unit representing allowed additional latency cost a tenant can spend to burst. 1 LBU approximates X ms of extra 95th latency on the pool given current load and model profile.
- Curator headroom: real-time estimate of remaining LBUs the pool can safely absorb before SLO is endangered.
- Mode: allow | temper | reroute | deny.
  - allow: process on dedicated pool normally (burst accepted).
  - temper: lower fidelity (quantized execution / lower prefix cache share) or increase batching window to reduce pressure; tenant sees degraded latency/cost tradeoff.
  - reroute: redirect to compatible fallback (hosted or cheaper variant) with controlled latency delta.
  - deny: reject or queue the request with 429/backoff.

High-level design:
1) Inputs:
  - per-tenant request rate, concurrency, and request size distribution (token length).
  - per-model latency profile map (model x seq_len -> baseline p50/p95/p99).
  - real-time pool telemetry: GPU utilization, queue depth, empirical tail latencies, KV cache hit rate.
  - tenant-configured burst-policy (max-LBUs/day, preferred fallback, latency sensitivity tag).

2) Core controller loop (approx):
  - compute current pool safety margin: available_LBUs = pool_budget - current_consumed. Pool_budget is derived from SLO headroom and real-time telemetry (sliding window).
  - for incoming request: estimate expected LBU_cost = latency_delta_estimate(request, model) * risk_factor(requestor).
  - if expected_cost <= tenant_remaining_LBUs and expected_cost <= available_LBUs -> allow.
  - if expected_cost <= tenant_remaining_LBUs but expected_cost > available_LBUs -> temper or reroute according to tenant policy and system heuristics.
  - if expected_cost > tenant_remaining_LBUs -> deny or suggest queued retry.

3) Temper strategies (ordered preference):
  - micro-batching: add short (<= 30ms) batching window for low-latency-tolerant routes to improve aggregate throughput.
  - fidelity shim: execute a quantized variant (faster kernel) with small quality tradeoff.
  - cache reallocation: temporarily reduce per-tenant KV cache share to free memory for hot prefixes (applies only if tenant-owned caches are used).

4) Reroute options:
  - internal fallback model within pool (lower cost/faster arch).
  - cross-pool spill to a Dedicated pool with spare headroom (same tenancy tier).
  - hosted fallback (Redwood API) with controlled latency expectations and customer notice.

Accounting and billing implications (ops note):
- LBUs are metered and reported on invoices as a separate usage line item (visibility but no immediate price change in v1).
- Tenants can purchase additional LBU bundles or opt into higher baseline SLO tiers that increase pool_budget.

API surface and admin controls (initial):
- tenant.burst_policy: {max_lbus_daily: int, preferred_fallback: enum, temper_allowed: bool, latency_tag: low|medium|high}
- pool.config: {base_SLO_ms_95: int, emergency_buffer_LBUs: int}
- admin endpoints: force_drain_pool(), snapshot_pool_state(pool_id), simulate_burst(tenants:list, duration_s:int)

Observability and telemetry (must-haves):
- real-time dashboard: pool LBU consumption (live & 1h/24h), top consuming tenants, per-tenant LBU balance, temper/reroute/deny counters.
- latency impact heatmap: pre/post-burst p50/p95/p99 per tenant and per-model.
- alerting: pool headroom < 20% and trend negative -> P0 on-call paging; repeated reroutes for same tenant -> ops ticket.

Runbook snippets (for SRE):
- if pool headroom drops precipitously: enable temporary pool-wide tempering_mode = true (soft throttle at 80% of LBU budget) and notify tenants via status page.
- if cascading tail latency spikes persist after tempering: initiate cross-pool spill to predefined spare pool and scale up warm nodes.
- for noisy tenant repetition: mark tenant for isolation review and apply temporary quota reduction / scheduled soft-quarantine.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- mis-estimated model latency profiles -> conservative default LBUs and fast feedback loop to recalibrate using live samples.
- telemetry lag -> use short conservative smoothing windows (10–30s) and fail-safe to temper rather than allow.
- runaway LBU consumption (attack) -> circuit breaker trips after X% of daily bundle consumed in <Y seconds.

Safety and privacy considerations:
- curator decisions are metadata-only; we never expose another tenant’s telemetry. Aggregated telemetry for billing only.
- reroute to hosted endpoints must respect tenant data residency flags; some customers with strict Private policies will have reroute disabled by default.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (research + simulation, 2 weeks): build simulator that replays real traces and validates LBU math vs historical latency regressions.
- Phase 1 (canary, 4 weeks): enable LBSC in allow+observe mode (decisions logged but not enforced) on two low-util pools. Tune risk_factors and estimate errors.
- Phase 2 (soft-enforce, 6 weeks): enable tempering for a subset of customers that opt-in; expose LBU meters in console. Close monitoring and daily checkpoints with SRE.
- Phase 3 (gradual opt-out enforcement): enable full enforcement on new pools and opt-in migrations; provide tenant opt-up purchasing path.

Success metrics (SLOs for this project):
- reduce pool-level p95 regression during 99th percentile burst events by >= 40% vs baseline.
- keep pooled p99 latency within configured SLO 99% of minutes in 30-day window during mixed workloads.
- reduce rate of full-pool evictions by 60% in canary pools.
- tenant satisfaction: fewer unexpected 429s vs credit-only approach (measure via CS tickets).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to map LBU to dollars? (Ops: visible metering first; pricing team later.)
- Granularity: per-request LBU accounting may be expensive; should we charge per-batch or per-second observed latency increase?
- How to pick default risk_factor for new tenants with no history? Conservative defaults vs rapid learning.
- Interaction with autoscaler: when to prefer scale-up vs tempering? Propose: autoscaler hints to curator (expected sustained rise triggers scale-up; short sharp spikes prefer tempering).

Engineering notes / initial tasks (rough):
- telemetry: produce real-time derived metric pool_available_LBUs (SRE + infra).
- modeling: latency_delta_estimate function per model/seq_len (Applied ML).
- control-plane: implement LBSC decision API and tenant policy storage (Product + Platform Eng).
- console: LBU meters and tenant-facing UI for policy (Developer Experience).
- billing: add LBU metering line in usage pipeline (Finance).

Appendix: simulator quick notes
- use 30-day historical traces sampled from top-50 pools; simulate varying tenant mixes and injection of synthetic noisy tenants. Measure predicted vs actual tail latency with and without temper.
- initial LBU calibration uses p95 slope heuristics: delta_LBU = k * (expected_p95_delta_ms), k tuned per-hardware-class.

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This is intentionally conservative: prefer temper/reroute over immediate tenant eviction.
- Want feedback on temper strategies ordering and acceptable micro-batch window (we flagged 30ms as conservative starting point).
- Also want pointers on product naming — LBUs might be confusing; alternatives: Surge Credits, Latency Credits, Burst QoS Units.

Unresolved action items:
- Priya: prototype latency_delta estimator PR by 2024-11-15.
- Ethan: small-scale simulator run and initial dashboard mocks by 2024-11-22.
- Daniel (owner): coordinate stakeholder review with SRE/product/finance 2024-11-25.
